background.definition: PF is an inflammatory process occurring in the plantar fascia and/or at its origin on the calcaneus causing plantar heel pain.

list.listitem: PF affects up to 10% of US population.
PF is the most common cause of inferior heel pain, especially in adults between the ages of 40 and 60 years and in runners.
PF accounts for up to 15% of all foot symptoms in adults requiring professional care.
No specific cause has been identified.
Repetitive microtrauma is a likely contributor evidenced by the relatively high incidence among runners.
A systematic review of 16 studies found that increased plantar flexion range of motion, higher BMI, and higher body mass were the strongest risk factors for PF.
Cumulative overload stress causing degenerative changes and inflammatory changes to the plantar fascia.
PF most commonly occurs near origin of plantar fascia from the medial calcaneal tuberosity.
Proper footwear, stretching exercises, and gradually increasing the intensity of exercise may decrease the risk of PF. C
The diagnosis of PF is based on patient history and characteristic physical findings. C
Imaging not generally useful in making the diagnosis of PF. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Calcaneal tenderness and swelling, abnormal imaging studies
Typically in adolescents, involves growth plate
Pain is typically retrocalcaneal, worse with activity
Foot pain is more diffuse, may have nighttime pain
Pain, paresthesias on sole of foot

list.listitem: The presence of characteristic findings in the history and physical examination is the key to making the diagnosis in most patients with PF.
PF presents in adults with plantar heel pain with weightbearing, especially with the first few steps after getting out of bed in the morning or after a period of inactivity.
The pain is often described as throbbing or piercing.
The pain usually improves with activity but may worsen with prolonged ambulation or other weightbearing activities.
Examination findings may include tenderness over the plantar fascia (or plantar aponeurosis) near the medial calcaneal tuberosity, as well as 1 to 2 cm distally along the plantar fascia.
Imaging is not generally useful in making the diagnosis except when trying to exclude other possible diagnoses.
Plain radiographs and bone scans may be useful in distinguishing PF from calcaneal stress fracture, but are generally not needed in most circumstances.
PF is associated with calcaneal spurs, but the clinical significance of this association is unclear.

A study obtained MRI of the calcaneal attachment of the plantar fascia in 77 asymptomatic volunteers, and found that calcaneal spurs, soft-tissue edema, and signal intensity changes in the fascia are common. Their presence should not be used to diagnose plantar fasciitis.
PF is diagnosed in adults with plantar heel pain with weightbearing, especially with the first few steps upon getting out of bed in the morning or after a period of inactivity.
Pain may be described as throbbing or piercing.
Pain usually improves with activity but may worsen with prolonged ambulation or other weightbearing activities.
Examination findings may include tenderness over the plantar fascia (or plantar aponeurosis) near the medial calcaneal tuberosity, as well as 1 to 2 cm distally along the plantar fascia.
Plantar fasciitis can generally be reliably diagnosed using characteristic historical and physical findings.
Use imaging when trying to rule-out other causes of inferior heel pain, such as calcaneal stress fractures.
Orthotics, night splints, and extracorporeal shock wave therapy are minimally, if it all, more effective than stretching exercises or no treatment. B
A local steroid injection may provide mild, short-term symptom relief. Autologous blood-derived products and extracorporeal shock-wave therapy may also effectively relieve pain.B
Surgery may benefit a small subset of patients with severe, persistent symptoms. C
A local steroid injection appears to provide some short-term pain relief, but minimal long-term benefit and cannot be routinely recommended.
There have been no studies specifically demonstrating the efficacy of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs in PF.

A 2015 meta-analysis found that autologous blood-derived products (especially platelet-rich plasma injections) and steroid injections were the most effective for providing relief at 3 months, while shock-wave therapy and autologous blood-derived products provided the most relief at 6 months. However, studies of platelet rich plasma were generally small and at high risk of bias. A second meta-analysis of 9 studies specifically comparing corticosteroid injection with autologous whole blood (excluding platelet rich plasma studies) found that corticosteroids provided somewhat better short-term results, and whole blood slightly better long-term results. Another meta-analysis of 15 studies again found that most were low quality, and concluded that corticosteroids were similar to platelet-rich plasma in the short term, and that PRP provided greater benefit at 6 to 12 months.

More recent meta-analyses found that shock-wave therapy especially at higher intensities was more effective than other modalities including steroid injections and ultrasound in reducing pain in patients with symptoms lasting at least 6 months. Although there are a few small studies that indicate low-level laser therapy may also be an effective treatment for pain, the studies were limited in numbers and by short duration of follow up (only up to 3 months).
Extracorpeal shock wave therapy is no more effective than custom orthotics or a 12 week exercise program.
More evidence is needed to assess the benefit of hypertonic dextrose injection (prolotherapy.)

A small (n = 75) but apparently well designed RCT randomized patients to platelet-rich plasma, corticosteroid (40 mg methylprednisolone) or saline injections. At 3 weeks and 3 months, both active therapy groups had large improvements in pain and function compared with placebo, which had none.
Mixed results have been found for extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ECSW).
In chronic PF, ECSW may have success rates between 50% and 65% when using focused higher energy levels without local anesthesia.
There is limited evidence that surgical options such as fascial release may be helpful for patients with persistent severe symptoms.
Nonmagnetic insoles are as effective as costlier magnetic insoles in terms of pain reduction in PF.
A single small randomized placebo controlled trial found an improvement in pain with a series of low level laser therapy (635 nm).
A meta-analysis of 6 studies found low-quality and heterogeneous evidence that dry needling reduces the intensity of pain in patients with PF.

Meta-analysis of 5 randomized trials of orthotics for treatment of plantar fasciitis found limited evidence of benefit. A different study found that while orthotics may help with pain, neither soft or hard customized orthotics improved function.
Stretches designed to specifically target the plantar fascia were more effective than general Achilles stretches in a systematic review of 8 studies.
Stretching is at least as effective as either custom or prefabricated orthotics.
It is uncertain if night splints providing ankle dorsiflexion are effective.
A rigorous "high load" strength training regimen is superior to stretching at 3 months, with faster short-term relief of pain, but the two interventions show similar improvement at 6 and 12 months.

A small study looking at the effect of adding low-dye Kinesio taping to extracorporeal shock wave therapy found that while taping seemed to improve foot function, it did not result in decreased pain or heel tenderness.
Most patients with PF experience symptom resolution within 12 months. C
Use of proper footwear, gradually increasing the intensity and duration of running, and stretching exercises may decrease the risk of developing PF.
More than 80% of patients with PF experience resolution of symptoms within 12 months.
